Raw child rollout JSONL—not the task names, UI labels, or agent self-reports—showed:\n-> \n-> - all three children had a non-empty `session_meta.parent_thread_id` linking them to the same parent;\n-> - all three had `agent_role = null`;\n-> - all three recorded `turn_context.model = \"gpt-5.6-sol\"`.\n-> \n-> Thus `task_name` only labeled the child path; it did not select the matching agent profile. This creates a material auditability risk: a child can be named “Terra” or “Luna” while actually consuming Sol.\n-> \n-> Expected: V2 should expose a supported typed-agent/profile selector and apply the selected profile's model, reasoning effort, sandbox, and instructions. The resolved model should remain directly verifiable in the child rollout metadata.\n-> \n-> Privacy note: local usernames, project names, absolute paths, thread/session IDs, and usage totals are intentionally omitted because they are not needed to reproduce the schema/inheritance bug.\n-...\n-> I believe the documented workaround fixes custom-role resolution and rollout\n-> metadata, but may not fix the model actually used for inference.\n-> \n-> Environment:\n-> \n-> - Codex CLI: 0.144.1\n-> - Parent: gpt-5.6-sol\n-> - Multi-agent version: v2\n-> - Custom role: luna_high\n-> - Configured child model: gpt-5.6-luna\n-> - Configured effort: high\n-> \n-> Configuration:\n-> \n-> ```toml\n-> [features.multi_agent_v2]\n-> enabled = true\n-> hide_spawn_agent_metadata = false\n-> tool_namespace = \"agents\"\n-> ````\n-> \n-> The expanded `agents.spawn_agent` tool successfully accepts:\n-> \n-> ```text\n-> agent_type = luna_high\n-> ```\n-> \n-> The child rollout records appear correct:\n-> \n-> ```text\n-> agent_role = luna_high\n-> model = gpt-5.6-luna\n-> reasoning_effort = high\n-> multi_agent_version = v2\n-> ```\n-> \n-> \n-> \n-> However, independent inspection of the actual model-request traffic shows that\n-> the child inference requests still use `gpt-5.6-sol`:\n-> \n-> \n-> \n-> \n-> \n-> All observed requests are Sol requests, including the turns correlated with the\n-> luna_high child.\n-> \n-> This suggests the role-specific model is applied to the local resolved config\n-> and persisted rollout metadata, but is later replaced or ignored when the\n-> actual inference request is constructed or dispatched.\n-> \n-> This may be a\n-\n----\n-\n-Title: Multi-Model Orchestration with OpenCode: Building Your AI Development Team | Fernando Nogueira's technical blog\n-URL: https://fernando-nog.netlify.app/multi-model-orchestration-opencode/\n-Published: 2026-07-29T00:00:00.000Z\n-Author: Fernando Nogueira\n-Highlights:\n-You have probably noticed that not all AI models are equally good at everything. Claude is great at reasoning through architecture.\n-...\n--5.6 Sol excels at generating code. A smaller model like Haiku is fast and cheap for quick\n-...\n-2.7\n-...\n-is purpose-built for coding at a fraction of the cost.\n-...\n-OpenCode’s agent system lets you do exactly that. You can configure multiple specialized agents, each with its own model, its own system prompt, and its own permissions. One agent plans. Another implements. A third reviews. And a fourth researches external documentation. All orchestrated by a primary agent that delegates work intelligently.\n-...\n-OpenCode has two types of agents: primary agents and subagents.\n-...\n-Subagents are specialized assistants that primary agents can invoke for specific tasks. OpenCode ships with three built-in subagents: General (full access, multi-step tasks), Explore (read-only, codebase search), and Scout (read-only, external docs research).\n-...\n-The key insight: every agent can have its own model. You are not stuck with one model for everything.\n-...\n-```markdown\n----\n-description: Analyzes requirements and creates implementation plans\n-mode: subagent\n-model: openai/gpt-5.6-sol\n-permission:\n-  edit: deny\n-  bash: deny\n----\n-...\n-Uses a coding-specialized model to write the actual code. This is where Kimi K2.7 Code shines — it is purpose-built for code generation at a fraction of the cost of frontier models.\n-...\n-```markdown\n----\n-description: Implements code changes based on an approved plan\n-mode: subagent\n-model: moonshot/kimi-k2.7-code\n-permission:\n-  edit: allow\n-  bash: allow\n----\n-...\n-Uses a fast, cheap model to review code changes. It should never modify code — only read and provide feedback.\n-...\n-```markdown\n----\n-description: Reviews code changes for quality, security, and best practices\n-mode: subagent\n-model: anthropic/claude-haiku-4-20250514\n-permission:\n-  edit: deny\n-  bash:\n-    \"git diff *\": allow\n-    \"git log *\": allow\n-    \"*\": deny\n----\n-...\n-Uses a model with web access to look up documentation, APIs, and external references.\n-...\n-```markdown\n----\n-description: Researches external documentation, APIs, and dependencies\n-mode: subagent\n-model: openai/gpt-5.6-terra\n-permission:\n-  edit: deny\n-  bash: deny\n-  webfetch: allow\n-...\n-Now we need a primary agent that knows how to delegate to these specialists. We will configure the Build agent to use a strong reasoning model and give it permission to invoke our subagents.\n-...\n-Add this to your `opencode.json` (merge with your existing config, do not replace it):\n-...\n-```json\n-{\n-  \"agent\": {\n-    \"build\": {\n-      \"model\": \"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5\",\n-      \"permission\": {\n-        \"task\": {\n-          \"*\": \"deny\",\n-          \"architect\": \"allow\",\n-          \"implementer\": \"allow\",\n-          \"reviewer\": \"allow\",\n-          \"researcher\": \"allow\"\n-        }\n-      }\n-    }\n-  }\n-}\n-```\n-...\n-This configuration does three things:\n-...\n-1. Sets the Build agent to use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the orchestrator model\n-2. Denies access to all subagents by default (`\"*\": \"deny\"`)\n-3. Explicitly allows only our four custom subagents\n-...\n-The orchestrator will now automatically delegate to the right specialist based on the task. When you ask it to implement a feature, it will invoke the architect first, then the implementer, then the reviewer — each using the model you configured for that role.\n-...\n-3. The orchestrator delegates. You will see it invoke the architect subagent to read the codebase and create a plan. Then the implementer writes the code. Then the reviewer checks the diff.\n-...\n-You can also invoke subagents manually by typing `@` followed by the agent name:\n-...\n-- Better planning: A reasoning-heavy model like GPT-5.6 Sol or Claude Sonnet thinks deeper about architecture\n-- Cheaper implementation: A coding-specialized model like Kimi K2.7 Code costs 3-5x less per token than frontier models\n-- Faster reviews: A small model like Haiku reviews code in seconds at near-zero cost\n-- Focused research: A model with web access can look up documentation without cluttering the main session\n-...\n-And because each agent has its own permissions, you get safety for free. The architect and reviewer cannot modify files. The researcher cannot run commands. Only the implementer has full write access.\n-...\n--5.6-sol\n-\n----\n-\n-Title: Mirrowel/opencode-agent-variants\n-URL: https://github.com/Mirrowel/opencode-agent-variants\n-Published: 2026-05-29T16:52:09.000Z\n-Author: Mirrowel\n-Highlights:\n-**Model-specific OpenCode subagents without copy-pasting agent prompts.**\n-...\n-Let the main model call `general-light`, `explore-fast`, or any other generated variant through the normal `task` tool.\n-...\n-OpenCode Agent Variants creates model-specific versions of your agents without copying prompts by hand.\n-Use it when you want the main model to choose between agents like:\n-...\n-* `general` for the default or strongest model\n-* `general-light` for a cheaper/faster model\n-* `explore` for normal codebase exploration\n-* `explore-light` for routine exploration on a smaller model\n-...\n-The plugin adds generated variants to OpenCode's normal `task` tool list and provides one TUI wizard for editing the variant config.\n-...\n-OpenCode already has strong built-in agents, but model selection is usually attached to the current session or a hand-written agent config. That creates an awkward choice:\n-...\n-* Run every subagent on the expensive main model.\n-...\n-* Copy built-in prompts into custom agents and watch them drift from upstream.\n-* Tell the model when to use cheaper agents in prose and hope it follows the rule.\n-...\n-Agent Variants keeps the normal OpenCode flow: the assistant still calls `task` once, but the task list can contain purpose-built aliases such as `general-light` or `explore-glm`. Built-in variants route back to the native parent agent, so OpenCode keeps owning the prompt, permissions, tools, and mode.\n-...\n-After configuration,\n-...\n-agents with distinct names and descriptions:\n-...\n-```\n-general         Strong default reasoning agent.\n-general-light   Variant agent general-light. Runs general using GLM 5.1. Use this exact alias for routine low-cost work.\n-explore         Codebase exploration agent.\n-explore-heavy   Variant agent explore-heavy. Runs explore using GPT-5.5. Use this exact alias for deep verification or a second opinion.\n-```\n-...\n-When the model calls `task` with `general-light`, the plugin routes execution through the native `general` agent and applies the configured model override to the child session.\n-...\n-* Generate variants from existing agents with model, temperature, prompt, description, options, and color overrides.\n-...\n-* Keep OpenCode's built-in agent prompts and permissions up to date by routing built-in variants to their native parent agent.\n-* Create real copied variants for agents defined in config or markdown.\n-* Manage variants from a single TUI command: `Agent Variants: Configure`.\n-* Store all plugin settings in a sidecar file instead of editing `opencode.json` for every variant.\n-* Avoid agent-tool pollution: the plugin does not register management tools for\n-...\n-1. Create a variant from a subagent-capable parent, for example `general -> general-light` or `explore -> explore-light`.\n-2. Restart OpenCode again so the generated agent list is assembled at startup.\n-...\n-After that, the main model can call the generated variant through the normal `task` tool. No agent-facing management tools are added.\n-...\n-The wizard defaults to showing only subagent-capable parent agents when adding or editing parent entries. Agent Variants are meant for agents callable through OpenCode's `task` tool. You can temporarily show all agents from `Debug & advanced` if you need to inspect or repair existing config.\n-...\n-|Pattern|Example|Why use it|\n-|Basic retrieval work|`explore-basic`|Delegate file finding, symbol lookup, extraction, and bounded data gathering to Luna/nano-class models.|\n-|Balanced general work|`general-light`|Delegate routine edits or analysis to Terra/mini-class models that still provide moderate judgment.|\n-...\n-|Balanced code search|`explore-light`|Keep broader codebase reading off the strongest model without dropping to the basic retrieval tier.|\n-...\n-|Specialist model|`explore-gemini`, `general-glm`|Route specific task types to models that are strong or inexpensive for that shape of work.|\n-...\n-|Shared model aliases|`models.light`|Change the underlying model once and reuse it across multiple variants.|\n-...\n-|Agent source|Behavior|\n-|Built-in agents like `general` and `explore`|Virtual aliases route to the native parent, preserving upstream prompts and permissions.|\n-|Agents from `opencode.json` or `opencode.jsonc`|Variants are generated as copied config agents with overrides applied.|\n-|Markdown agents|Variants\n-...\n-generated from the configured markdown-backed agent definition.|\n-|Primary-\n-...\n-agents|Diagnostics warn because they are not callable through\n-...\n-`task` tool.|\n-...\n-Agent Variants is designed for subagents. It does not try to override OpenCode's main-session model picker.\n-...\n-Profiles are conditional overlays applied **on top of the global default**, activated manually or automatically by the primary session's selected model. They answer questions like \"when I'm on the flagship model, my explore agent should use a stronger model; when I'm on a budget model, everything downgrades\".\n-...\n-```\n-{\n-  routing: { /* activeProfile: \"sol-heavy\" (optional manual pin) */ },\n-  profiles: {\n-    \"sol-heavy\": {\n-      match: { model: \"zai/glm-5.3\", variant: [\"high\", \"max\"] }, // omitted variant = any\n-      agents: {\n-        general: {\n-          parent: { model: \"zai/glm-5.3\", variant: \"max\" },   // base calls + inherited default\n-          variants: { deep: { temperature: 0.9 } },            // specific variant overrides\n-        },\n-      },\n-    },\n-  },\n-}\n-```\n-...\n-* Activation: `match.model` (+ optional `variant` string or array) is checked against the primary session's current model; when several profiles match, the **last one wins**. A manual `routing.activeProfile` pin always wins over matching. `\"default\"` in a variant filter matches sessions without a variant selected. A profile without a `match` rule is **manual only** — it never activates automatically.\n-...\n-Variant names default to `${parent}-${variantKey}`. In the example above, `general` plus variant key `light` becomes `general-light`.\n-...\n-Variant descriptions are generated with selection guidance by default. The wizard can infer basic/light/heavy/verification/parallel/strict-review style guidance from the variant key, alias, model preset, resolved model name, model label, and provider model variant. Capability inference maps GPT nano and GPT-5.6 Luna to `basic`, GPT mini and GPT-5.6 Terra to `light`, and GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the bare `gpt-5.6` alias to `heavy`. Literal canonical tier words (`basic`, `light`, or `heavy`) are explicit overrides. Otherwise, recognized model capability wins over semantic names: a Sol-backed `data-entry` alias remains heavy, while `data-entry` can still infer basic when the model tier is unknown. You can also pick a built-in guidance preset during variant creation or press `ctrl+p` while editing the `Description` field to insert preset text. Press `i` on a preset to preview the full text it adds.\n-...\n-Built-in agents such as `general` and `explore` cannot be copied externally without vendoring OpenCode internals. For these agents, the plugin creates a virtual alias:\n-...\n-* The variant appears in the task tool list.\n-* The main model can call `task` once with the variant name.\n-* The plugin routes the call to the native parent before execution.\n-* The plugin applies configured model, request parameter, and explicit prompt overrides.\n-* The plugin keeps routing metadata internal and exposes only a small natural alias hint in the task title.\n-* By default, child-session correlation uses OpenCode task metadata instead of prompt markers. A legacy prompt-marker fallback can be enabled from `Debug & advanced` if needed.\n-...\n-This preserves native prompts and permissions. The child session may internally show the parent agent name for built-in variants; that is expected.\n-...\n-Use Agent Variants when you want cheaper subagent routing, cleaner task-agent names, less prompt drift, and fewer duplicated custom agents while keeping OpenCode's native behavior intact.\n-\n----\n-\n-Title: Sub-agent Surface (v1 / base / v2) | opencodex\n-URL: https://opencodex.me/guides/sub-agent-surface/\n-Published: N/A\n-Author: N/A\n-Highlights:\n-Surface (v1 / base / v2)\n-...\n-opencodex\n-...\n-A sub-agent is a separate Codex worker that the main agent can create for a focused task. It has its own context and tools, so several independent tasks can run in parallel. opencodex controls which Codex collaboration surface exposes those workers, which models Codex offers for them, and how a failed model can fall back. It does not decide when your main agent must delegate.\n-...\n-| Mode |\n-...\n-Codex gets | Who should pick it |\n-| --- | --- | --- |\n-| v1 |\n-...\n-namespaced `spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `resume_agent`,\n-...\n-`close_agent` tools. A spawn can select another model directly. | Beginners who need\n-...\n-across different providers, especially native-to-routed children. |\n-...\n-| base (default) | Upstream model pins: GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra use v2, Luna uses v1, and unpinned models follow Codex’s `multi_agent_v2` feature flag. | Most users. It follows Codex’s intended surface for each model without forcing one globally. |\n-...\n-| v2 | Flat `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `interrupt_agent`, and agent-list tools, with concurrent sessions. | Users who want the newer concurrent workflow and understand model inheritance and the encrypted-task limitation below. |\n-...\n-On v2, an optional Keep ChatGPT on v1 switch (`keepNativeChatGptOnV1`) leaves Sol/Terra on the v1 surface so they can still spawn Grok or Claude. ChatGPT-native parents encrypt v2 `NEW_TASK` bodies; routed models cannot read them. Routed parents stay on v2, where child tasks are plaintext. This is a switch inside v2, not a fourth catalog mode.\n-...\n-Start with base. Choose v1 when cross-provider delegation must work predictably. Force v2 only when you specifically want its newer session model across every catalog entry.\n-...\n-- v1 stamps `multi_agent_version = \"v1\"` on every model.\n-- base restores upstream pins. Unpinned entries follow the native `multi_agent_v2` feature flag.\n-- v2 stamps `multi_agent_version = \"v2\"` on every model, except when Keep ChatGPT on v1 is enabled: ChatGPT-native rows stay `\"v1\"` and routed or combo rows stay `\"v2\"`.\n-...\n-For a v2 roster, eligibility has three states: an entry stamped `\"v2\"`, explicitly set to `null`, or with no `multi_agent_version` field is eligible. A genuine `\"v1\"` pin is excluded because it states that the model belongs to the other collaboration surface.\n-...\n-- `injectionModel` is the preferred worker model named in opencodex guidance.\n-- `injectionEffort` is the optional `reasoning_effort` to request for that model.\n-- `injectionPrompt` replaces the built-in v2 guidance text.\n-...\n-These are instructions to the main agent, not a proxy-side spawn router. On v2, a full-history fork inherits the parent model and rejects model or effort overrides. Guidance therefore tells Codex to use `fork_turns: \"none\"` (or a positive partial turn count such as `\"3\"`) when passing `model` or `reasoning_effort`, and to make the task message self-contained.\n-...\n-1. The requested primary model.\n-2. A per-model chain from `subagentModelFallbackByModel` in opencodex config, keyed by the requested primary model.\n-3. The global `subagentModelFallback` list in opencodex config.\n-...\n-- Dashboard → first stat cell: choose v1, base, or v2.\n-- Models → top-row segmented control: choose the same global mode.\n-- Dashboard → Sub-agent delegation: set guidance model/effort and the native-default opt-in.\n-- Subagents: choose and order the roster and configure the global fallback chain.\n-...\n-Use `ocx agent` for delegation, roster, effort-cap, and fallback settings:\n-...\n-Terminal window\n-\n-ocx agent status\n-\n-ocx agent injection set --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 --effort xhigh\n-\n-ocx agent subagents set gpt-5.6-sol,anthropic/claude-sonnet-5\n-\n-ocx agent fallback set gpt-5.4-mini,xai/grok-4.5 --poll-ms 60000\n-\n-ocx agent effort set --subagent max\n-...\n-| Endpoint | Manages |\n-| --- | --- |\n-| `/api/v2` | Surface mode, native feature flag, and thread settings |\n-| `/api/injection-model` | Preferred model, effort, custom prompt, guidance, and native-default sync |\n-| `/api/effort-caps` | Main-agent and sub-agent effort ceilings |\n-| `/api/subagent-models` | Ordered roster of up to five models |\n-| `/api/subagent-model-fallback` | Global fallback order and poll interval |\n-...\n-No. Guidance can recommend a model, and native-default sync can provide a Codex default, but the main agent still decides whether to delegate.\n-...\n-A full-history v2 fork inherits the parent model. Use a spawn that sets `fork_turns` to `\"none\"` or a positive partial count before passing a model or effort override.\n-...\n-It may be picker-hidden, outside the five-model display limit, missing from the catalog, or pinned to v1. A `\"v2\"`, `null`, or absent surface value is eligible; a real `\"v1\"` pin is not.\n-...\n-`injectionEffort` affects only delegated-worker guidance and, when explicitly enabled, native Codex sub-agent defaults. It does not change the parent session’s effort. `ultra` is a client-facing top tier that Codex converts to `max`; opencodex then maps or clamps the value for the selected provider.\n-...\n-model context cap is independent of sub-\n-...\n-mode. Configure it on the\n-...\n-real context windows.\n-...\n-Last updated: Aug 20, 2026\n-```\n-\n-**Tool: webfetch**\n-\n-**Input:**\n-```json\n-{\n-  \"url\": \"https://opencode.ai/docs/zen/\",\n-  \"format\": \"markdown\"\n-}\n-```\n-\n-**Output:**\n-```\n-Zen | OpenCode     [Skip to content](#_top)\n-\n-  [![](/docs/_astro/logo-dark.DOStV66V.svg) ![](/docs/_astro/logo-light.B0yzR0O5.svg) OpenCode](/docs/)\n-\n-[app.header.home](/)[app.header.docs](/docs/)\n-\n-[](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode)[](https://opencode.ai/discord)\n-\n-Search CtrlK\n-\n-Cancel\n-\n--   [Intro](/docs/)\n--   [Config](/docs/config/)\n--   [Providers](/docs/providers/)\n--   [Network](/docs/network/)\n--   [Enterprise](/docs/enterprise/)\n--   [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/)\n--   [Windows](/docs/windows-wsl)\n--   Usage\n-    \n-    -   [Roles](#roles)\n-    -   [Model access](#model-access)\n-    -   [Bring your own key](#bring-your-own-key)\n--   [Goals](#goals)\n-\n-# Zen\n-\n-Curated list of models provided by OpenCode.\n-\n-OpenCode Zen is a list of tested and verified models provided by the OpenCode team.\n-\n-Zen works like any other provider in OpenCode. You login to OpenCode Zen and get your API key. It’s **completely optional** and you don’t need to use it to use OpenCode.\n-\n----\n-\n-## [Background](#background)\n-\n-There are a large number of models out there but only a few of these models work well as coding agents. Additionally, most providers are configured very differently; so you get very different performance and quality.\n-\n-Tip\n-\n-We tested a select group of models and providers that work well with OpenCode.\n-\n-So if you are using a model through something like OpenRouter, you can never be sure if you are getting the best version of the model you want.\n-\n-To fix this, we did a couple of things:\n-\n-1.  We tested a select group of models and talked to their teams about how to best run them.\n-2.  We then worked with a few providers to make sure these were being served correctly.\n-3.  Finally, we benchmarked the combination of the model/provider and came up with a list that we feel good recommending.\n-\n-OpenCode Zen is an AI gateway that gives you access to these models.\n-\n----\n-\n-## [How it works](#how-it-works)\n-\n-OpenCode Zen works like any other provider in OpenCode.\n-\n-1.  You sign in to **[OpenCode Zen](https://opencode.ai/auth)**, add your billing details, and copy your API key.\n-2.  You run the `/connect` command in the TUI, select OpenCode Zen, and paste your API key.\n-3.  Run `/models` in the TUI to see the list of models we recommend.\n-\n-You are charged per request and you can add credits to your account.\n-\n----\n-\n-## [Endpoints](#endpoints)\n-\n-You can also access our models through the following API endpoints.\n-\n-Model\n-\n-Model ID\n-\n-Endpoint\n-\n-AI SDK Package\n-\n-GPT 6 Product objective\n-\n-The application must answer:\n-\n-> “Using the information available at this cutoff, what is the estimated probability this stock rises or falls by the target close, and what sizes of move are plausible?”\n-\n-### Required MVP capabilities\n-\n-| ID | Requirement |\n-|---|---|\n-| R01 | Search by company name or ticker and freely switch between stocks and ETFs |\n-| R02 | Use the most recent eligible Yahoo Finance data, with visible timestamps and freshness |\n-| R03 | Produce close-to-close forecasts |\n-| R04 | Produce intraday-to-close forecasts |\n-| R05 | Display direction probabilities, movement thresholds, conditional gains/losses, and prediction intervals |\n-| R06 | Provide a polished, responsive dashboard with historical charts |\n-| R07 | Route all frontend application-data access through the API |\n-| R08 | Record and search every submitted query, including repeated and failed requests |\n-| R09 | Preserve original forecasts, their inputs, and subsequent outcomes |\n-| R10 | Provide verified SQLite backups and restoration |\n-| R11 | Meet security, correctness, and laptop-performance acceptance criteria |\n-| R12 | Pass Playwright MCP browser acceptance and automated regression tests |\n-| R13 | Provide reproducible setup, documentation, CI, and published Git revisions |\n-\n-**Both forecast modes belong in the completed MVP.** A daily-only dashboard is an intermediate milestone.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 2. Verified environment and constraints\n-\n-| Component | Observed environment |\n-|---|---|\n-| Architecture | ARM64 / `aarch64` |\n-| CPU | 8 cores, Cortex-A55 and Cortex-A76 |\n-| Memory | 6.5 GiB |\n-| Swap | None |\n-| Workspace filesystem | 10 GiB total; approximately 5.9 GiB free during inspection |\n-| OS | Debian 12 |\n-| Python | 3.11.2 |\n-| SQLite | 3.40.1 with full-text search support |\n-| Node.js | Not currently available on `PATH` |\n-| Git remote | `https://github.com/eddiesoz/stock_probs.git` |\n-\n-The repository currently contains prototype scripts, including a broken Yahoo Finance script, and a committed Python virtual environment.\n-\n-### Design implications\n-\n-- One application service and one SQLite database.\n-- Bounded network concurrency.\n-- Incremental data acquisition and caching.\n-- Serial browser testing on the laptop.\n-- Controlled backup and diagnostic-artifact retention.\n-- Project-local, locked development dependencies.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 3. SOL subagent orchestration\n-\n-### Coordinator\n-\n-The primary agent owns:\n-\n-- Task decomposition and dependency order.\n-- Acceptance criteria and file ownership.\n-- Dispatching and resuming subagents.\n-- Resolving disagreements between Build and QA.\n-- Roadmap status and evidence tracking.\n-- Git staging, commits, pushes, and release verification.\n-\n-### Three available SOL roles\n-\n-| Role | Responsibilities | Ownership |\n-|---|---|---|\n-| **`sol-build`** | Implement application behavior, migrations, integrations, and focused developer tests; repair QA findings | Assigned application/configuration files and unit/integration tests |\n-| **`sol-qa`** | Independently verify requirements, review changes, maintain acceptance tests, operate Playwright MCP, and report defects | Acceptance tests and QA evidence; application changes return to Build |\n-| **`sol-docs`** | Document verified setup, API behavior, model behavior, operational procedures, and changes | Assigned documentation files |\n-\n-All three profiles will explicitly select **GPT-5.6 Sol** using the verified identifier for the authenticated provider.\n-\n-OpenCode documents `opencode/gpt-5.6-sol` for its Zen provider. The current local configuration contains no SOL role profiles, so model availability and actual subagent model selection must be verified during bootstrap.[1]\n-\n-### Orchestration limits\n-\n-- Up to **three subagents per task**, one per role.\n-- At most three active subagents across the project initially.\n-- One implementation workstream at a time on this laptop.\n-- Reuse the same role sessions during repairs.\n-- Subagents do not create additional subagents.\n-- Only the coordinator performs Git publication and changes acceptance status.\n-\n-### Parallel work and handoff\n-\n-At task start:\n-\n-- Build implements.\n-- QA prepares independent acceptance cases and fixtures.\n-- Documentation prepares the relevant document structure.\n-\n-After Build supplies a stable handoff:\n-\n-- Build pauses changes to the files under verification.\n-- QA tests that specific source revision.\n-- Documentation checks the actual implementation and verified commands.\n-- QA findings return to Build.\n-- Any behavior change invalidates the affected acceptance evidence.\n-\n-Only QA controls the acceptance browser during a verification session. Shared files, such as manifests and the roadmap, have one designated writer.\n-\n-### Task packet\n-\n-Every delegated task receives:\n-\n-```text\n-Task ID and objective\n-Requirement IDs\n-Dependencies and relevant design decisions\n-Assigned files\n-Acceptance criteria\n-Required verification commands and MCP journeys\n-Expected outputs\n-Known constraints\n-```\n-\n-Every role returns a concise report with changed files, evidence, unresolved issues, and handoff instructions.\n-\n-**A Build agent’s completion claim is not sufficient for acceptance.**\n-\n----\n-\n-## 4. Application architecture\n-\n-```text\n-Browser\n-  ├── HTML/CSS/JavaScript\n-  └── HTTP requests to /api/v1/*\n-                 │\n-                 ▼\n-              FastAPI\n-                 │\n-                 ▼\n-         Application services\n-          ├── Yahoo adapter\n-          ├── Forecast engine\n-          ├── Outcome evaluation\n-          └── Database repository\n-                       │\n-                       ▼\n-                     SQLite\n-```\n-\n-### Stack\n-\n-| Layer | Technology |\n-|---|---|\n-| Backend | FastAPI, one Uvicorn worker |\n-| Frontend | Jinja2 page shells, CSS, small JavaScript modules |\n-| Charts | Locally served Chart.js |\n-| Market data | yfinance behind an application-owned adapter |\n-| Numerical work | NumPy/pandas, SciPy where useful |\n-| Trading schedules | `exchange_calendars` |\n-| Database | Python `sqlite3` |\n-| Python dependencies | `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` |\n-| Browser tooling | Project-local npm package and lockfile |\n-| Agent browser testing | Official Playwright MCP server |\n-| Regression tests | pytest and Playwright Test |\n-| Code checks | Ruff, mypy, dependency vulnerability checks |\n-\n-### Mandatory API boundary\n-\n-The frontend obtains forecasts, prices, query history, exports, and backup status through the API.\n-\n-SQL, database connections, provider calls, and database files belong to the backend. Database and backup directories are outside publicly served paths.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 5. API contract\n-\n-| Endpoint | Responsibility |\n-|---|---|\n-| `POST /api/v1/searches` | Record and execute a company/ticker search |\n-| `POST /api/v1/forecasts` | Validate a forecast request, obtain inputs, calculate, and persist |\n-| `GET /api/v1/forecasts/{id}` | Return an original saved forecast |\n-| `GET /api/v1/history` | Search and paginate submitted queries |\n-| `GET /api/v1/instruments/{id}/prices` | Return historical price data |\n-| `GET /api/v1/exports` | Export selected records through validated filters |\n-| `GET /api/v1/backups/status` | Return backup status |\n-| `GET /api/v1/health` | Support readiness checks |\n-\n-Forecast responses include:\n-\n-- Instrument identity, exchange, and currency.\n-- Requested mode and effective mode.\n-- Reference price and observation timestamp.\n-- Data-fetch timestamp and freshness.\n-- Target session and close time.\n-- Probabilities, thresholds, and prediction intervals.\n-- Sample size and data-quality status.\n-- Model/configuration version.\n-- Saved forecast identifier.\n-\n-Errors use consistent codes and readable messages. Pagination, query sizes, and sorting are bounded and validated.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 6. Yahoo Finance data pipeline\n-\n-```text\n-Record request\n-  → Resolve instrument\n-  → Check cache and market schedule\n-  → Fetch eligible data\n-  → Validate and normalize\n-  → Save forecast input snapshot\n-  → Calculate forecast\n-  → Persist result\n-  → Return API response\n-```\n-\n-### Data handling\n-\n-- Retrieve daily history on demand, up to ten years where available.\n-- Retrieve five-minute history for intraday analysis.\n-- Store market-observation time separately from download time.\n-- Preserve exchange timezone, currency, and corporate actions.\n-- Exclude incomplete bars from completed-period calculations.\n-- Identify missing sessions rather than treating gaps as ordinary one-day returns.\n-- Verify the price-adjustment policy with split and dividend fixtures.\n-- Preserve genuine large moves while identifying corrupt or inconsistent data.\n-- Resolve the exchange calendar explicitly; unsupported schedules produce a clear status.\n-\n-### Freshness and failure behavior\n-\n-- Refresh daily data when another session may have completed.\n-- Refresh intraday data at bounded intervals while relevant.\n-- Pause frontend polling when the page is hidden.\n-- Coalesce duplicate in-flight provider requests.\n-- Apply timeouts and limited backoff.\n-- Preserve cached results with their actual timestamps.\n-- Backfill available gaps when the laptop resumes.\n-\n-Yahoo five-minute history is limited to approximately 60 calendar days in yfinance’s implementation. The local archive will grow as data is collected; gaps beyond the provider’s retention remain identifiable.[2]\n-\n----\n-\n-## 7. Forecast definitions and model\n-\n-### A. Close-to-close\n-\n-**Reference:** the latest completed trading session’s close.\n-\n-**Target:** the next trading session’s close.\n-\n-The initial model will compare:\n-1. An empirical historical distribution.\n-2. A volatility-adjusted historical distribution.\n-\n-The volatility-adjusted model:\n-\n-- Calculates historical returns.\n-- Estimates volatility causally.\n-- Standardizes historical shocks.\n-- Rescales those shocks to the current volatility estimate.\n-- Derives all probabilities and intervals from one consistent distribution.\n-\n-Filtered historical simulation is suitable for a lightweight numerical implementation, but its quality depends on the volatility estimate and available history.[3]\n-\n-### B. Intraday-to-close\n-\n-**Reference:** the newest eligible completed five-minute bar.\n-\n-**Target:** the upcoming regular-session close.\n-\n-Use historical returns from comparable intraday cutoffs to their session closes, respecting exchange-local time and session type.\n-\n-When no fresh eligible regular-session observation exists, show a closed-market or stale-data state and identify the available daily forecast.\n-\n-Intraday sample sizes are smaller. Minimum-data criteria and uncertainty must be visible, especially for rare large moves.\n-\n-### C. Outputs\n-\n-- Probability of rising, falling, or remaining unchanged.\n-- Median predicted percentage move.\n-- Conditional median gain and conditional median loss.\n-- 50%, 80%, and 95% prediction intervals.\n-- Initial thresholds of ±1%, ±3%, ±5%, and ±10%.\n-- Equivalent price levels in the instrument’s currency.\n-\n-These describe outcomes **at the target close**. Intraday barrier-touch probabilities would require a separately defined model.\n-\n-### D. Historical reconstruction\n-\n-The interface distinguishes:\n-\n-- **Saved forecast:** the result actually recorded at that time.\n-- **Historical reconstruction:** a calculation performed later using a historical cutoff.\n-\n-Yahoo can revise historical data. Saved input snapshots establish what this application used; a later reconstruction cannot establish exactly what Yahoo originally served.\n-\n-### E. Model evaluation\n-\n-Use chronological walk-forward evaluation and a separate final evaluation period.\n-\n-Report:\n-- Direction and threshold Brier scores.\n-- Reliability plots.\n-- Prediction-interval coverage.\n-- Baseline comparisons.\n-- Sample counts and evaluation dates.\n-\n-No future prices, current retrospective metadata, or future corporate-action information may enter historical features improperly.\n-\n-Volatility adjustment primarily affects move magnitude and tail risk. Additional directional models should be introduced only after demonstrating value in out-of-sample evaluation.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 8. Frontend experience\n-\n-### Dashboard\n-\n-- Company/ticker search with identity confirmation.\n-- Forecast-mode selection.\n-- Historical cutoff controls.\n-- Reference price, target close, and freshness.\n-- Direction-probability cards.\n-- Threshold table.\n-- Prediction-interval and distribution displays.\n-- Historical-price chart.\n-- Model and sample-size details.\n-\n-### History\n-\n-- Search by original text, company, and symbol.\n-- Filter by date, mode, and status.\n-- Reopen original results.\n-- Compare forecasts with observed outcomes.\n-- Start a fresh analysis from a previous query.\n-- Export CSV/JSON.\n-\n-### Design acceptance\n-\n-- Responsive desktop and narrow-screen layouts.\n-- Keyboard-accessible controls.\n-- Readable contrast and typography.\n-- Optional dark mode.\n-- Numerical summaries for charts.\n-- Clear loading, error, empty, stale-data, and insufficient-history states.\n-\n-Charts are downsampled for rendering while calculations retain full eligible data.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 9. SQLite persistence and backups\n-\n-### Core records\n-\n-| Record | Contents |\n-|---|---|\n-| Instruments | Canonical symbol, company, exchange, currency, timezone |\n-| Market bars | Daily/intraday OHLCV, actions, timestamps, provenance |\n-| Queries | Original input, parameters, timestamps, status, failure information |\n-| Input snapshots | Immutable, compressed, deduplicated forecast inputs |\n-| Forecasts | Saved results, reference/target times, model version |\n-| Outcomes | Observed returns and scoring results |\n-\n-Every submitted search, analysis, reconstruction, and refresh is recorded. Deliberately repeated submissions remain distinct. Autocomplete keystrokes are interface activity rather than submitted queries.\n-\n-### Database behavior\n-\n-- Explicit transactions and foreign keys.\n-- Short writes; provider calls outside transactions.\n-- Thread-owned connections.\n-- Busy timeout.\n-- Versioned SQL migrations.\n-- Indexed filters and full-text search.\n-- No automatic expiry of query history.\n-\n-Start with rollback-journal mode. This suits the workload and avoids relying on WAL behavior in the installed SQLite version, which falls within the documented WAL-reset issue’s affected range.[4]\n-\n-### Backup acceptance\n-\n-- Automatic backup when due while the app is running.\n-- Backup before migrations.\n-- Manual backup command.\n-- SQLite online backup API.\n-- Integrity checks before marking a backup successful.\n-- Configurable destination, retention, and disk limits.\n-- Restore while the application is stopped.\n-- Browser verification of restored history.\n-\n-Git stores source revisions. SQLite backups preserve application data.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 10. Security and performance\n-\n-### Security\n-\n-- Bind to `127.0.0.1`.\n-- Validate Host/Origin and protect state-changing requests.\n-- Use parameterized SQL and allowlisted sort fields.\n-- Validate symbol syntax, input lengths, dates, and thresholds.\n-- Escape user/provider text.\n-- Serve scripts locally under a restrictive Content Security Policy.\n-- Keep databases, backups, logs, secrets, and caches outside static paths.\n-- Use restrictive data-file permissions.\n-- Sanitize spreadsheet exports.\n-- Pin dependencies and run vulnerability checks.\n-- Keep restore operations in the local CLI.\n-\n-### Performance targets\n-\n-Measure on this laptop:\n-\n-| Measurement | Proposed target |\n-|---|---|\n-| Normal application-server memory | Below 500 MiB |\n-| Cached single-symbol forecast | Below one second |\n-| Indexed history search on 100,000-query fixture | Below 250 ms |\n-| Idle behavior | Negligible background CPU consumption |\n-\n-Network latency and browser-test resource usage are recorded separately.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 11. Playwright MCP acceptance\n-\n-### Setup\n-\n-Use the official **`@playwright/mcp`** server through OpenCode’s local MCP integration.\n-\n-- Install a supported ARM64 Node.js LTS runtime.\n-- Pin MCP and browser-test dependencies under `tools/browser/`.\n-- Register the server in `opencode.json`.\n-- Configure headless Chromium explicitly.\n-- Use isolated browser profiles and a dedicated acceptance database.\n-- Validate browser/tool compatibility on ARM.\n-- Capture session evidence and bounded diagnostic artifacts.\n-- Restart OpenCode after configuration changes.\n-\n-Playwright MCP is headed by default, making explicit headless configuration important.[5]\n-\n-### QA ownership\n-\n-`sol-qa` operates the MCP browser during acceptance. The coordinator verifies that the tools are actually available to that subagent and that the selected model is SOL.\n-\n-MCP unavailability or browser-launch failure blocks the relevant gate.\n-\n-### Test path\n-\n-```text\n-SOL QA agent\n-  → Playwright MCP\n-  → Headless Chromium\n-  → Real frontend\n-  → Real API\n-  → Real application services\n-  → Real temporary SQLite database\n-```\n-\n-Deterministic tests substitute data at the Yahoo adapter boundary. Browser/API/database behavior remains real.\n-\n-Final live-data checks use the actual Yahoo adapter.\n-\n-### Browser acceptance matrix\n-\n-| ID | Required behavior |\n-|---|---|\n-| B01 | Search by company name and select the correct instrument |\n-| B02 | Switch symbols without mixing results or history |\n-| B03 | Complete a daily forecast with correct displayed results |\n-| B04 | Complete an intraday forecast with correct reference and target times |\n-| B05 | Display populated charts, thresholds, and intervals |\n-| B06 | Run and correctly label historical reconstruction |\n-| B07 | Find successful, failed, and repeated queries |\n-| B08 | Restart and reopen an original forecast |\n-| B09 | Refresh data without changing an earlier saved result |\n-| B10 | Handle invalid symbols, missing data, rate limits, and stale data |\n-| B11 | Export and verify CSV/JSON contents |\n-| B12 | Restore a backup and retrieve restored history through the browser |\n-| B13 | Operate core flows by keyboard and at narrow viewport widths |\n-| B14 | Confirm API-mediated data access and inaccessible database files |\n-| B15 | Complete real-Yahoo daily and intraday user journeys |\n-| B16 | Identify uncaught browser errors and unexpected external dependencies |\n-\n-Successful data-rich scenarios must produce numerical forecasts. Error-state handling alone cannot satisfy forecasting acceptance.\n-\n-### Automated regression tests\n-\n-Alongside MCP acceptance:\n-- Python pytest covers numerical, API, and database behavior.\n-- Checked-in Playwright Test scenarios run in CI.\n-- MCP-driven QA covers interactive acceptance and diagnosis.\n-\n-**Both recorded MCP acceptance and automated regression checks are required.**\n-\n----\n-\n-## 12. Correctness tests\n-\n-Highest-priority tests include:\n-\n-1. Appending future prices cannot change an earlier forecast.\n-2. Yahoo cache updates cannot alter saved results.\n-3. Larger downside thresholds cannot have higher exceedance probabilities.\n-4. Up/down/unchanged probabilities sum to one.\n-5. Prediction intervals are ordered and use the displayed reference price.\n-6. Splits and currency-unit changes do not become artificial crashes.\n-7. Incomplete bars are excluded.\n-8. Session gaps do not become ordinary daily returns.\n-9. Intraday evaluation groups observations by session.\n-10. History survives restart and restore.\n-11. Interrupted and failed requests remain identifiable.\n-12. API validation and frontend/export handling resist injection.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 13. Repository layout and commands\n-\n-### Proposed layout\n-\n-```text\n-MVP-PLAN.md\n-MVP-ROADMAP.md\n-AGENTS.md\n-README.md\n-opencode.json\n-pyproject.toml\n-uv.lock\n-Makefile\n-\n-.opencode/agents/\n-  sol-build.md\n-  sol-qa.md\n-  sol-docs.md\n-\n-src/stock_probs/\n-  app.py\n-  cli.py\n-  services.py\n-  db.py\n-  providers/\n-  forecasting/\n-  templates/\n-  static/\n-\n-migrations/\n-tests/\n-tools/browser/\n-docs/\n-legacy/\n-.github/workflows/\n-```\n-\n-`AGENTS.md` will reference the plan and roadmap and contain only verified commands, boundaries, and repository-specific pitfalls.\n-\n-### Commands to implement\n-\n-| Command | Purpose |\n-|---|---|\n-| `make setup` | Install locked development dependencies |\n-| `make browser-install` | Install compatible Chromium and system prerequisites |\n-| `make dev` | Start the local application |\n-| `make check` | Format check, lint, typecheck, unit/API tests |\n-| `make browser-test` | Run deterministic browser regressions |\n-| `make acceptance` | Run deterministic acceptance, including restore tests |\n-| `make live-smoke` | Run explicit real-Yahoo verification |\n-| `make release-check` | Verify release evidence and required checks |\n-\n-MCP browser journeys are performed by QA through the configured tools. Task states and evidence\n-\n-### States\n-\n-```text\n-pending\n-  → in_progress\n-  → verifying\n-  → accepted\n-  → published\n-```\n-\n-Failures return work to implementation. Missing external prerequisites produce `blocked`.\n-\n-### Required task record\n-\n-```text\n-Task ID:\n-Requirement IDs:\n-Acceptance criteria:\n-Dependencies:\n-Build / QA / Documentation assignments:\n-Assigned files:\n-Status:\n-Verification commands:\n-MCP scenarios:\n-Tested source revision or working-tree identifier:\n-Observed results:\n-Artifact/report locations:\n-Outstanding defects:\n-Published checkpoint and CI URL:\n-```\n-\n-The coordinator owns status changes. Documentation may prepare evidence summaries, but acceptance requires QA results.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 16. Orchestrated acceptance loop\n-\n-### Step 1 — Select and define\n-\n-The coordinator:\n-- Selects a ready task.\n-- Confirms dependencies.\n-- Defines observable acceptance criteria.\n-- Assigns file ownership.\n-- Dispatches up to three SOL roles.\n-\n-### Step 2 — Build and prepare\n-\n-- Build implements.\n-- QA develops independent verification cases.\n-- Documentation prepares relevant updates.\n-\n-### Step 3 — Stable handoff\n-\n-Build reports:\n-- Files changed.\n-- Implemented behavior.\n-- Developer checks performed.\n-- Known limitations.\n-\n-Changes to the verification target pause.\n-\n-### Step 4 — Independent QA\n-\n-QA:\n-- Reviews the implementation against requirements.\n-- Runs focused tests.\n-- Exercises applicable flows through Playwright MCP.\n-- Inspects API/network behavior, browser errors, and persistence.\n-- Returns pass/fail findings with evidence.\n-\n-### Step 5 — Repair\n-\n-If QA fails:\n-- Coordinator creates explicit defect tasks.\n-- Build repairs the root cause.\n-- Documentation adjusts affected descriptions.\n-- QA reruns affected checks and the required regression gate.\n-\n-An unexplained intermittent pass is not sufficient. Repeated failures without a new diagnosis become a documented blocker rather than an endless blind retry loop.\n-\n-### Step 6 — Documentation verification\n-\n-Documentation confirms:\n-- Setup commands execute as documented.\n-- API behavior matches actual responses.\n-- Model terminology matches implementation.\n-- Backup and restore procedures match tested behavior.\n-- No unfinished functionality is described as complete.\n-\n-### Step 7 — Accept and publish\n-\n-The coordinator:\n-1. Reviews QA and documentation evidence.\n-2. Inspects Git status, diff, and recent commits.\n-3. Stages intended files.\n-4. Commits the checkpoint.\n-5. Pushes it.\n-6. Verifies the remote revision and CI.\n-7. Marks the checkpoint published.\n-\n-### Step 8 — Continue\n-\n-Advance to the next ready task. Regressions reopen affected tasks.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 17. Git and CI workflow\n-\n-Repository: [`eddiesoz/stock_probs`](https://github.com/eddiesoz/stock_probs).\n-\n-### Foundation work\n-\n-- Verify remote state and write access.\n-- Install/authenticate GitHub CLI as needed.\n-- Untrack virtual environments while preserving local installations.\n-- Exclude databases, backups, caches, browser binaries, dependencies, secrets, and generated artifacts.\n-- Preserve the prototype implementation under `legacy/`.\n-\n-### Checkpoint policy\n-\n-- Coordinator alone stages, commits, and pushes.\n-- Each checkpoint includes implementation, tests, and verified documentation.\n-- Browser-facing checkpoints require MCP evidence and passing browser regressions.\n-- CI failures reopen the relevant milestone.\n-- Release tags identify the accepted source version.\n-\n-Source-control publication and database backups are verified separately.\n-\n----\n-\n-## 18. No implementation milestone is complete.\n-9: - A task may move to **Completed** only after its acceptance evidence, verification result, repair history, and reviewer are recorded.\n-10: \n-11: ## Product Goal\n-12: \n-13: Build a small, auditable, local web application where a user selects a Yahoo Finance stock or ETF and receives two forecast views:\n-14: \n-15: 1. **Close-to-close:** a forecast from a clearly identified completed market-session close to the applicable next close.\n-16: 2. **Latest-completed-5-minute-bar-to-close:** a forecast from the latest completed five-minute bar available at request time to the applicable close. An in-progress bar must never be used as completed input.\n-17: \n-18: Each view must expose probabilities and magnitude intervals, not just a point estimate. Every displayed result must identify its symbol, asset type, input timestamps, provider/as-of time, forecast horizon, model/version, interval level and units, stale-data state, and any limitation or failure.\n-19: \n-20: This is a research and auditability tool, not a trading system or a promise of predictive accuracy.\n-21: \n-22: ## Non-Negotiable Boundaries\n-23: \n-24: ### API boundary\n-25: \n-26: - All frontend application data must pass through FastAPI `/api/v1`.\n-27: - The browser must not import a SQLite client, issue SQL, open a database path, or infer storage details from the API.\n-28: - The API owns validation, provider calls, forecast calculation, persistence, history queries, and backup/restore operations.\n-29: - API errors must be structured, safe to display, and specific enough to distinguish invalid input, unavailable market data, stale data, calculation failure, persistence failure, and restore failure.\n-30: \n-31: ### Data source and time semantics\n-32: \n-33: - Yahoo Finance is the planned market-data source for user-selected stocks and ETFs.\n-34: - The provider adapter must record the exact query, requested interval, returned coverage, timezone/session interpretation, response as-of time, and any missing or stale bars.\n-35: - The forecast service must reject or clearly label insufficient, stale, out-of-session, or ambiguous data. It must not silently substitute a different interval or session.\n-36: - Close-to-close and five-minute-bar-to-close calculations must have separate, testable horizon semantics. A request made outside market hours must follow a documented session rule rather than an implicit guess.\n-37: \n-38: ### Persistence and auditability\n-39: \n-40: - Every submitted search is an append-only audit event, including successful, failed, and repeated submissions. A repeated search may reuse a valid prior result, but the new submission event must still be stored.\n-41: - A successful forecast stores an immutable input snapshot: normalized symbol and asset type, request and source timestamps, selected bars, session/calendar interpretation, data-quality flags, model and algorithm version, parameters, thresholds, and provider metadata or content fingerprint.\n-42: - The immutable result stores probabilities, magnitude intervals, interval levels and units, calculation timestamps, and the input-record reference.\n-43: - An observed outcome is appended after the forecast horizon with the actual close/return, observation timestamp, comparison rule, and outcome state. It must not rewrite the original forecast input or result.\n-44: - Corrections require a new versioned record or audit event. No update-in-place behavior may erase what was originally submitted or displayed.\n-45: - History queries must be bounded, searchable, and served through `/api/v1`; the UI must not scan the database file.\n-46: \n-47: ### User experience\n-48: \n-49: - The dashboard must work at desktop and mobile widths without hiding essential status or controls.\n-50: - Every search control needs a visible label, keyboard path, focus state, validation message, loading state, empty state, success state, and failure state.\n-51: - Charts, colors, and interval bands must have text or table equivalents; color alone cannot communicate direction, confidence, stale data, or failure.\n-52: - History must support practical search/filtering and expose enough context to distinguish a repeated request from a new forecast.\n-53: - Accessible names, semantic structure, contrast, keyboard operation, reduced-motion behavior, and screen-reader announcements are acceptance concerns, not polish.\n-54: \n-55: ### Deployment and resources\n-56: \n-57: - The default service must bind to loopback only. The deployment must make any broader bind an explicit, documented, security-reviewed choice.\n-58: - Validate symbols, request sizes, date ranges, page sizes, backup paths, and provider timeouts at the API boundary.\n-59: - Do not expose provider credentials or local file paths to the browser or logs. Avoid unsafe CORS and unbounded concurrent provider calls.\n-60: - Keep the default process, query, cache, and browser-test footprint suitable for a low-resource ARM64 laptop. Measure rather than assuming that desktop-scale defaults are safe.\n-61: - All code must have useful comments for non-obvious model, time-window, persistence, security, and resource decisions.\n-62: \n-63: ## Planned Architecture\n-64: \n-65: The intended flow is browser dashboard -> frontend API client -> FastAPI `/api/v1` -> domain services -> Yahoo Finance adapter and server-owned SQLite repositories. The browser has no alternate path to storage or to Yahoo Finance.\n-66: \n-67: The API/application layers should remain separable:\n-68: \n-69: - **Transport:** FastAPI routes, request/response schemas, validation, safe error mapping, and API versioning.\n-70: - **Domain:** symbol selection, session/bar semantics, forecast calculation, interval formatting, stale-data policy, and outcome comparison.\n-71: - **Adapters:** Yahoo Finance retrieval, SQLite repositories/migrations, backup artifact handling, and clock/calendar boundaries.\n-72: - **Presentation:** responsive accessible dashboard, loading/error/empty states, results, and searchable history.\n-73: - **Quality:** unit, API, persistence, accessibility, security, performance, restore, and browser regression checks.\n-74: \n-75: The exact module names and endpoint names are implementation decisions for M01. The invariants above are not optional.\n-76: \n-77: ## Forecast Contract\n-78: \n-79: The forecast engine must make assumptions visible and reproducible. At minimum, a stored forecast must answer:\n-80: \n-81: - Which user-selected symbol and asset type were requested?\n-82: - Which completed close or five-minute bar was the origin, and which close was the target?\n-83: - What market timezone, trading-session rule, and provider response were used?\n-84: - What historical window, features, parameters, thresholds, and model/version produced the output?\n-85: - What probability definitions were used, such as direction or return threshold?\n-86: - What do the magnitude intervals mean, what confidence/coverage level do they represent, and are they expressed as percent return, price, or both?\n-87: - What data was missing, stale, unavailable, or outside the supported market session?\n-88: \n-89: The current hard-coded and dummy calculations are not acceptance evidence for this contract. M03 must replace or explicitly isolate them behind tested, versioned domain behavior and must not present mock backtests as validated forecasts.\n-90: \n-91: ## Task Register\n-92: \n-93: The coordinator assigns no more than three agents to a task in addition to the coordinator. Clark\n-Highlights:\n-Filtered historical simulation with an underlying GARCH process can be used as a valuable tool in VaR analysis, as it derives risk estimates that are sensitive to the distributional properties of the historical data of the produced predictive density. I examine the applications to risk analysis that filtered historical simulation can provide, as well as an interpretation of the predictive density as a poor man’s Bayesian posterior distribution. The predictive density allows us to make associated probabilistic statements regarding the results for VaR analysis, giving greater measurement of risk and the ability to maintain the optimal level of risk per tolerance in portfolios to remain compliant with regulations. Keywords: Filtered Historical Simulation, Predictive Density, Value at Risk, VaR, GARCH\n-...\n-Filtered historical simulation was first introduced by Barone-Adesi, Giannopoulos and Vosper (1999). It is a great method for determining VaR for portfolios, as it uses both nonlinear econo metric models and historical returns to build the predictive density that the portfolio could take for multiple days looking forward. Rather than most models, which suffer the problem of under estimating the risk of extreme outcomes, filtered historical simulation risk estimated are derived directly from the tails of the distribution. In filtered historical simulation, price series are not forced to conform to a probability distribu tion, but the data are allowed to speak for themselves. Historical data is still considered. This is an important aspect to filtered historical simulation since a basic Monte Carlo simulation only draws from a theoretical distribution, which smooths the empirical distribution and may underestimate the risk of catastrophe. It generates thousands of scenarios for the mean and variance of each risk factor in a multi-period horizon. This allows filtered historical simulation to provide a more accurate depiction of the tail structure in future prices. These features make filtered historical simulation very easy to implement in risk analysis and stress-testing. Filtered historical simulation works by using a parametric model of return volatility, such as a GARCH model, to simulate log returns over some predefined risk horizon. Using the estimated GARCH model\n-...\n-, filtered historical simulation will assume that GARCH draws from the standardized empirical distribution, so therefore the standardized innovations are et = rt/σˆt. rt represents the historical daily log return and σˆ2 t represents the GARCH daily standard deviation. The simulation process begins by setting initial conditions σ˜0 and r˜0. r˜0 will be set equal to the log return from the previous day, but there are at least two different options for setting σ˜0. The first of the two options is setting σ˜0 equal to the last estimated daily conditional volatility from the GARCH model. The second option is to set σ˜0 equal to the long run unconditional volatility:\n-...\n-To calculate the VaR through filtered historical simulation, first I need to estimate a GARCH model to account for volatility clustering patterns as seen above. I used the optimizer ‘rugarch’ from R to optimize the GARCH parameters ωˆ , αˆ, and βˆ. These are the estimated parameters that were used in the i.i.d. bootstrap process for filtered historical simulation. The full S&P 500 and IBM code can be found in the linked Github Repository (Clark, Tyson (2019)). As is shown by Mc Donald (2009), there are jumps in the return data for IBM surrounding earnings announcements that the GARCH model has difficulty explaining, so those 5 particular dates have been omitted from the optimization process. After the optimizer has found the values of ωˆ , αˆ, and βˆ, they can be used in the i.i.d. bootstrap process of filtered historical simulation. I will first find the scaled volatility adjusted VaR using the GARCH process to compare my results in filtered historical simulation.\n-...\n-As is shown in this table, the adjusted GARCH model overestimates risk when compared to filtered historical simulation. This is because the square root scaling of a daily VaR model estimated through GARCH doesn’t allow for mean reversion, and will subsequently overestimate the VaR when taken on a day with a higher than usual variance. This is why it is important to use the statistical bootstrap, and why filtered historical simulation is better than a simple square root adjustment to a single day GARCH estimation. This will hold in almost all of the 10,000 simulations carried out. We can see this distribution in the produced predictive density. My simulated predictive density is shown below.\n-...\n-This produced predictive density helps us see the distribution of returns through a bootstrap of 10,000 simulations. This distribution can be quite useful when a bank or investment manager is looking at the VaR for his or her respective portfolio. The density is computed using frequentist methods, but can be looked at as a poor-man’s Bayesian posterior distribution when there is an uninformed prior, as is most likely the case with a VaR model (Murphy (2012)). In fact, the way filtered historical simulation is modeled, it is very similar to a Bayesian model. Without getting too involved in the Bayesian perspective, Bayes’ rule can be defined as:\n-...\n-, where P(θ) is the prior applied to the Bayesian model. It can be seen that when this prior is uninformed, it will drop out, leaving just P(x| θ), which will be informed by the model just as filtered historical simulation. It is shown here that the actual VaR model is being computed using frequentist methods, but this produced density is the frequentist approach to a Bayesian posterior. I would like to quote Terry Speed about how ‘We don’t need to be Bayesian; we just need to be approximately so. We don’t need theory to tell us our method works; we just need to simulate and see’ (Speed (2011)). This Bayesian interpretation can be important. In ‘Computer Age Statistical Inference’, Efron and Hastie provide some comparisons between frequentist methods and Bayesian methods (Efron and Hastie (2016)). An important note they make is that a Bayesian places a large bet on his or her prior being correct, or at least not harmful, but a frequentist will take a more defensive approach, that by statistical methods he or she can produce a useful distribution, regardless of the true µ. In the perspective of filtered historical simulation for VaR, this is an important point since there can be no prior belief regarding the distribution of returns if one wants to properly account for risk, especially in the tails. Though calculated using frequentist method, the distribution shown above is very close to a Bayesian posterior distribution. When a risk manager or trader is thinking about risk, they can’t think about these frequentist models. Though the models may do a good job of summarizing data, the true uncertainty must be thought of from a subjective sense. Filtered historical simulation produces a predictive density that allows traders and risk managers to do just that. Though filtered historical simulation is a fre quentist method, rarely, if ever, is the produced distribution thought of from a Bayesian subjective sense, though that is exactly what the model is producing. This way of thinking about uncertainty incorporates the theory that prices reflect information, or tacit knowledge, rather than just being something that is calculated through a model (Hayek (1945)). This way of thinking will help risk managers and traders more properly account for risk in their models, and is a great way to look at filtered historical simulation.\n-...\n-(Barone-Adesi, Giannopoulos and Vosper (1999)). In contrast to some other techniques where the scenarios are generated ad hoc, FHS uses a combination of nonlinear econometric models and past returns to build the probability distribution of possible values that the asset (risk factor) could take in the days ahead. Risk estimates are directly derived from the tails of the distribution. \n-\n-The FHS is a kind of historical simulation since uses past returns as innovations in modeling the randomness of the asset prices. It has however one major improvement; the row returns are first scaled by the volatility that prevailed that day and then are multiplied by the current forecast of volatility. The first pass, the scaling, is necessary in order to make the past returns stationary and to render them suitable innovations for a simulation process. The second step, the re-scaling, endows the historical returns to reflect the current volatility conditions prevailing in the markets.\n-...\n-From the statistical perspective the FHS is seen as a semi-parametric model. The price series is not forced to conform to any kind of probability distribution, but rather the data are allowed to talk themselves. Risk estimation is highly dependent on good prediction of uncommon events, or catastrophic risk. Simulation models that draw innovations from theoretical distributions, such as the parametric Monte Carlo, indeed smooth the empirical distribution of the data and consequently they may underestimate \"catastrophic risk\" \n-\n-The cross dependencies among the series are handled through parallel bootstrapping. This reduces dramatically the dimensions of the problem because the number of parameters and the time needed to carry out the computation increases linearly with the number of securities or risk factors in the portfolio. In contrast, in models that are relying on the variance-covariance matrix to capture the cross dependencies, the dimension is a quadratic function of the number of securities that are handled.\n-...\n-In summary, the FHS combines\n-...\n-best features from other risk management models. \n-\n-- The data do not have to follow a unique or a pre-specified distribution (it uses the historical or empirical distribution). Thus it allows for fat tails, volatility clusters and changing means.\n-- It goes around the bias problem of using just historical data.\n-- It handles easily dependencies across very large numbers of assets.\n-...\n-- Generates thousands of scenarios for the mean and variance of each risk factor in a multi-period horizon. This provides a more accurate formation of the structure in the tails of possible price realizations. \n-- Non linear instruments such options are re-priced each day ahead in the risk horizon. The re-pricing handles the risk with unbalanced portfolios found in the expiring contracts before the end of the investment horizon.\n-...\n-- Stress testing, sensitivity analysis and coherent risk measures are easily implemented.\n-\n----\n-\n-Title: Predictive Distributions via Filtered Historical Simulation for ...\n-URL: https://digitalcommons.usu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2394&context=gradreports\n-Published: N/A\n-Author: Tyson Clark\n-Highlights:\n-Filtered historical simulation with an underlying GARCH process can be used as a valuable tool in VaR analysis, as it derives risk estimates that are sensitive to the distributional properties of the historical data of the produced predictive density. However, recent studies (Kuester et al. 2006) have found that the distribution used in the filtering stage can influence the VaR estimates obtained in the context of this methodology. Using Extreme Value Theory (EVT) this paper explains that the VaR estimates for lower probabilities should not be sensitive to the distribution assumed in the filtering stage of the FHS method. However, for higher probabilities, the EVT results do not hold and therefore the use of alternative distributions might impact the VaR estimates. These theoretical results are tested using both simulated and real data. Three different realistic data generating processes were considered to generate several series of simulated returns. Additionally, three competing models, differing in the innovations assumption, were tested: a normal-GARCH, a t-GARCH and a skew-t-GARCH. Our backtesting results indicate that FHS can forecast VaR with accuracy for data which exhibits a high incidence of zeros, time-varying skewness, asymmetric effects to return shocks on volatility, as well as other stylized facts. Importantly, our results for the simulated data demonstrate that, for lower probabilities, the choice of the distribution assumed in the filtering stage has no impact on the performance of FHS as an accurate method to forecasting VaR. Additionally, 40 years of daily data on six well known active stock indices are used to empirically evaluate the FHS VaR estimates. Four competing GARCH-type specifications, combined with three different innovation assumptions (normal, Student-t and skew-Student t), are used to capture time series dynamics. Based on a sample of several VaR probabilities, the results of the dynamic quantile (DQ) tests clearly indicate that the use of asymmetric GARCH models (specifically GJR and GJR in Mean) generally improve the VaR forecasting performance of FHS. In addition, the choice of a skew-Student t distribution for the innovation process slightly improves the performance results of the GJR in Mean model. When different VaR probabilities are used, the choice of an appropriate model specification seems to be more important than the choice of a suitable distribution assumption. With respect to the lower VaR probability tested (1%), the results show that, as expected, the VaR estimate is very similar regardless of the GARCH model and distribution assumed.\n-\n----\n-\n-Title: Filtered Historical Simulation, Explained | Quant Memo\n-URL: https://quantmemo.com/concepts/filtered-historical-simulation\n-Published: N/A\n-Author: N/A\n-Highlights:\n-Keep the real shape of historical shocks, but rescale each one to reflect today's volatility instead of the volatility on the day it happened. It fixes historical simulation's biggest flaw, that it treats a calm year and a crisis year the same.\n-...\n-Plain historical simulation replays the actual returns from the last one or two years, unweighted, unscaled, exactly as they happened. That works fine when volatility has been roughly stable. It works badly the moment volatility has changed: a calm return from a quiet stretch is treated as equally informative as a calm return would be today, even during a period when volatility has doubled, and a crash return from a stressed period gets treated as no more or less likely to repeat than it should be right now. Filtered historical simulation fixes the mismatch by rescaling every historical return to today's volatility before replaying it.\n-...\n-A tailor altering an old suit for a client does not just hand over\n-...\n-suit as it was\n-...\n-body; she takes the suit's pattern, its shape and proportions, and rescales it to today's measurements. The pattern (where the shoulders taper, how the waist narrows) is preserved; only the scale changes. The C function in this section, designed to be called by a background thread or process for creating a backup of an online database, avoids these problems using the following approach: \n-\n-1. If there are still more pages to copy from database pDb, then the function sleeps for 250 milliseconds (using the sqlite3_sleep() utility) and then returns to step 2. \n-4. The instinct — `cp app.db backup.db`, or `shutil.copy2`, or a filesystem snapshot — produces a file that opens without complaint and passes casual inspection, yet is silently torn: the copy captures the main database file at one instant and misses the committed frames still living in the `-wal` file, or captures a page mid-write. It walks the source database page by page under the source’s own locking rules, so the target is a transactionally consistent image even though writers never stopped. This topic sits inside the Backup, Recovery & Data Integrity guide and assumes the source is already running in Write-Ahead Logging mode with a hardened busy_timeout in place. Here we cover exactly how to drive `sqlite3.Connection.backup()`, how to throttle it so it never starves the write path, and how to prove the copy is sound before you trust it.\n-...\n-The Backup API is a small state machine exposed in Python as `sqlite3.Connection.backup(target, *, pages=-1, progress=None, name=\"main\", sleep=0.250)`. It opens a backup handle between a source connection and a target connection, then copies database pages from source to target in steps. Each call to the underlying `sqlite3_backup_step()` copies up to `pages` pages; passing `pages=-1` copies everything in a single step, while a positive value copies that many pages and returns, letting you loop. Between steps the source database is unlocked, so writers can commit. This is the entire reason the API is safe to run hot: it never holds a long read lock, and it tracks writes that land on already-copied pages so the final image is consistent as of the moment the copy completes.\n-...\n-Before copying anything, confirm the source is in a state where a hot copy is meaningful. Confirm the source timeout and that a `sleep` is set so the driver yields between retries:\n-...\n-```python\n-timeout = src.execute(\"PRAGMA busy_timeout;\").fetchone()[0]  # ms the step waits before raising\n-assert timeout >= 5000, f\"busy_timeout too low for a hot backup: {timeout} ms\"\n-```\n-...\n-Fallback: Raise `busy_timeout` on the source connection and set a non-zero `sleep` on the `backup()` call so busy steps retry politely. The timeout-sizing method is in Busy Timeout Configuration.\n-...\n-```sql\n-PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE);  -- checkpointed_pages stuck far below log_pages => a reader is pinning the WAL\n-```\n-...\n-- Confirm the source is in `wal` mode before choosing the online API over a copy-under-read-transaction.\n-- Run the backup from a dedicated connection that is not also serving writes.\n-- Set `pages` and `sleep` from the workload table; never use `pages=-1` on a busy source.\n-- Attach a `progress` callback and treat a rising `remaining` as a restart warning.\n-- Pre-flight target free space at ~1.2× the source size to avoid `SQLITE_FULL`.\n-- Raise `busy_timeout` on the source so busy steps wait instead of raising.\n-- Run `PRAGMA integrity_check` on the finished target and require `ok` before trusting it.\n-- Write the target to storage that does not share an I/O queue or flash region with the source.\n-- Delete partial target\n-\n----\n-\n-Title: SQLite: Wal-Mode Blocking Locks\n-URL: https://sqlite.org/src/doc/tip/doc/wal-lock.md\n-Published: N/A\n-Author: N/A\n-Highlights:\n-SQLite: Wal-Mode Blocking Locks\n-...\n-On some Unix-like systems, SQLite may be configured to use POSIX blocking locks by:\n-...\n-- building the library with SQLITE_ENABLE_SETLK_TIMEOUT defined, and\n-- configuring a timeout in ms using the sqlite3_busy_timeout() API.\n-...\n-## Wal Recovery\n-...\n-Wal database \"recovery\" is a process required when the number of connected database clients changes from zero to one. In this case, a client is considered to connect to the database when it first reads data from it. Before recovery commences, an exclusive WRITER lock is taken.\n-...\n-Without blocking locks, if two clients attempt recovery simultaneously, one fails to obtain the WRITER lock and either invokes the busy-handler callback or returns SQLITE_BUSY to the user. With blocking locks configured, the second client blocks on the WRITER lock.\n-...\n-With blocking locks configured, the only cases in which clients should see an SQLITE_BUSY error are:\n-...\n-- if the OS does not grant a blocking lock before the configured timeout expires, and\n-- when an open read-transaction is upgraded to a write-transaction.\n-...\n-In all other cases the blocking locks implementation should prevent clients from having to handle SQLITE_BUSY errors and facilitate appropriate transfer of priorities between competing clients.\n-...\n-Clients that lock multiple databases simultaneously must be wary of deadlock.\n-```\n-\n-**Tool: bash**\n-\n-**Input:**\n-```json\n-{\n-  \"command\": \"git count-objects -vH && git ls-tree -l HEAD && git ls-remote origin HEAD\",\n-
